issues.legal_issue: An unregistered private arbitration award that declares a pre-existing interest in immovable property, rather than creating or extinguishing that interest, is not compulsorily registrable and may be relied on as evidence of the pre-existing interest.
material_facts: Two brothers jointly funded the purchase of a house, each contributing half of the purchase price, although the sale certificate was issued only in one brother’s name.
A private arbitration award declared that the brother named on the sale certificate had held the property as benamidar and that both brothers had owned equal shares from the date of purchase.
The award was made a rule of court years before the named brother entered into the sale agreement concerning the property.
The evidence showed joint mutation and joint possession and enjoyment of the property.
issues.conclusion: The award declared the appellant’s pre-existing half share and did not create a new interest in the property. It was therefore not compulsorily registrable, and the appellant could rely on it as evidence of his ownership.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1)(b) and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, a non-testamentary instrument that creates, declares, assigns, limits, or extinguishes an interest in immovable property of the prescribed value must be registered, and an unregistered instrument required to be registered cannot affect the property or be received as evidence of a transaction affecting it. Whether registration is required depends on what the instrument purports to do: an instrument creating or extinguishing an interest is registrable, but one that merely declares a pre-existing interest is not. An unregistered award is not inadmissible for every purpose and may be relied on to show resolution of a dispute and the parties’ acceptance or conduct. The Court relied on Lachhman Dass v. Ram Lall, Satish Kumar v. Surinder Kumar, Ratan Lal Sharma v. Purshottam Harit, Uttam Singh Duggal v. Union of India, Kashinathsa Yamosa Kabadi v. Narsingsa Bhaskarsa Kabadi, Champalal v. Samarath Bai, Addanki Narayanappa v. Bhaskara Krishtappa, CIT v. Juggilal Kamalapat, and Kale v. Dy. Director of Consolidation.

rule.if: property_title_dispute and private_arbitration_award and award_declares_preexisting_interest and joint_contribution_to_purchase and named_titleholder_was_benamidar

predicates.property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over a claimed interest in immovable property.
predicates.private_arbitration_award: The parties referred their dispute to private arbitration and an award was made.
predicates.award_declares_preexisting_interest: The award describes an interest in the property as already existing rather than as newly created or extinguished by the award.
predicates.joint_contribution_to_purchase: The person claiming an interest contributed to the purchase price together with the person named in the title document.
predicates.named_titleholder_was_benamidar: The person named in the title document held the property on behalf of the other contributor as well as himself.

issues.definition: When a property-title dispute concerns a private award declaring a jointly funded, pre-existing interest held through a benamidar, the award is not compulsorily registrable.

issues.legal_issue: A contract for the sale of an entire divisible property by a person who owns only part of it and lacks the consent of a co-owner cannot support specific performance against the non-consenting co-owner, but may be specifically enforced as to the seller’s share.
material_facts: The seller contracted to sell the entire house, but the appellant owned half of it and had not consented to the sale.
The house was divisible, and the sale agreement did not bind the appellant as to his half share.
The purchaser and her husband were neighbours, and the property’s joint mutation and joint possession provided indications of joint ownership.
The courts below ordered specific performance of the contract for the entire property.
issues.conclusion: The decree for specific performance of the entire property was erroneous. The contract could be specifically enforced only in respect of the seller’s half share, and not against the appellant’s share.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20(1) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary; that discretion must be exercised on sound and reasonable judicial principles, considering the circumstances, the parties’ conduct, and their respective interests. Section 12(1) generally bars specific performance of only part of a contract, but Section 12(4) permits it where the part that can and ought to be performed stands on a separate and independent footing from the part that cannot or ought not to be performed. Section 10(b) concerns whether monetary compensation would afford adequate relief. Applying these provisions, the Court held that equity and justice required partial enforcement because the property was divisible and the seller could not contract on behalf of the non-consenting co-owner.

rule.if: appeal_from_specific_performance_decree and contract_covers_entire_property and seller_owned_only_part and noncontracting_coowner_did_not_consent and property_is_divisible and joint_ownership_was_apparent_to_purchaser

predicates.appeal_from_specific_performance_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree granting specific performance of a property-sale contract.
predicates.contract_covers_entire_property: The sale contract purports to cover the whole property.
predicates.seller_owned_only_part: The seller held only a part share in the property.
predicates.noncontracting_coowner_did_not_consent: A co-owner who was not a party to the contract did not agree to the sale of that co-owner’s share.
predicates.property_is_divisible: The property can be divided so that the seller’s share can be dealt with separately.
predicates.joint_ownership_was_apparent_to_purchase: Circumstances available to the purchaser indicated that the property was jointly owned or possessed.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a decree for sale of an entire divisible property, but the seller owns only part, a non-contracting co-owner did not consent, and joint ownership was apparent to the purchaser, specific performance is limited to the seller’s share.
